names: Union Iron Works Foundry and Warehouse
summary: The oldest surviving shipyard buildings at Pier 70: the 1885-86 brick Machine Shop and blacksmith/boiler shop (113/114, joined by a 1914 concrete connector, 492 ft long) and the 1916-17 reinforced-concrete foundry and warehouse (115/116) beside it. Closed and red-tagged in 2001, they were rehabilitated by Orton Development with a buckling-restrained-brace steel system and public atrium, receiving certificates of occupancy in November 2017 (115/116) and April 2018 (113/114), and were subleased to Uber Advanced Technologies Group and Gusto.

milestones.text: Eastern portion of Building 113/114 (blacksmith and boiler shop) completed to civil engineer D. E. Melliss's design; western portion (machine shop) completed 1886
The two brick buildings joined by a reinforced concrete and steel connector
Contract of almost $100,000 awarded for the new one-story reinforced concrete foundry (Building 115), under construction by June 1916; Bethlehem's plans date 115/116 to 1917
Machine shop closed by the Port and red-tagged for its hazardous unreinforced-masonry condition, after use for ship repair until then
Port Commission endorses the Pier 70 Preferred Master Plan (Resolution 10-27), which calls for a National Register district and rehabilitation of the 20th Street buildings

Port Commission awards the 20th Street Historic Buildings opportunity to Orton Development after a 2011 RFP; Exclusive Negotiating Agreement approved April 2012; term sheet endorsed October 2012 (Board of Supervisors December 2012)

Historic Preservation Commission informational hearing on the rehabilitation of the ten 20th Street Historic Buildings (case 2013.1168E): ~270,000 gsf existing plus ~69,000 gsf of new mezzanines, ~334,000 gsf total
Union Iron Works Historic District listed in the National Register of Historic Places (NRIS 14000150), giving the project access to federal historic tax credits
Port Commission Resolution 14-33 approves the Lease Disposition and Development Agreement and 66-year Master Lease (L-15814) with Historic Pier 70, LLC (Orton) and adopts CEQA findings
Master lease approved by the Board of Supervisors and fully executed, giving Orton site control; construction commences thereafter (September 2015 per the National Trust)
Permanent financing for the Historic Core project achieved

Port Commission update: six of eight buildings complete, Buildings 101 and 102 still under construction, project 100% subleased except two atrium retail spaces; total cost revised from $81.9M to an estimated $127.0M
Historic Shipyard at Pier 70 Rehabilitation receives a Governor's Historic Preservation Award
Building 113 stabilized after two magnitude-4.0 earthquakes in summer 2015
Gusto sublease of Building 113 East (49,074 sq ft) commences, ten years, office
Otto (Uber's self-driving truck unit) reported leasing 130,000 sq ft, taking the Historic Core to 85% occupancy
Certificate of occupancy for Buildings 115/116; Uber Advanced Technologies Group sublease of Buildings 114, 115 and 116 (79,771 sq ft, ten years, PDR) commences
Uber Advanced Technologies Group sublease of Building 113 West (51,299 sq ft, two years, office) commences
Certificate of occupancy for Buildings 113/114
Two small retail spaces in the Building 113 atrium still available; Orton begins activating the atrium and plaza with events

costs.what: Hard cost of the Building 113/114 rehabilitation (2018 actual; $24.2M for 113 and 114 combined at 2014 approvals)
Hard cost of the Building 115/116 rehabilitation (2018 actual; $7.1M combined at 2014 approvals)
Contract for the new foundry (Building 115) in January 1916 ('almost $100,000')

facts.value: Orton Development, Inc. through Historic Pier 70, LLC (66-year master lease L-15814 from the Port of San Francisco)
Marcy Wong Donn Logan Architects (design architect); Mark Hulbert, Preservation Architecture (historic architect)

Developer equity up to $14 million plus loans; Port participation rent of 50% of revenues above debt and a 14% equity return; sources in 2018: Port capital $1.8M, Seismic Safety Loan $23.6M, historic tax credit equity $20.4M, private debt and equity $81.2M
Contributing resource to the Union Iron Works Historic District (NRHP, listed April 17, 2014)
Dr. D. E. Melliss, civil engineer (113/114); designer of 115/116 not recorded
113/114: 492 ft by 175 ft 6 in by 62 ft tall; 115/116: 218 ft by 174 ft by 57 ft 2 in
113/114: 89,686 (NRHP), 95,157 before and 129,228 after rehabilitation (Port); 115/116: 33,858 (NRHP), 38,694 before and 53,625 after (Port)

New perimeter steel framing at two levels stabilizes the unreinforced brick walls (up to 18 inches out of plumb); buckling-restrained braced frames provide lateral resistance; new interior steel frame and mezzanines
Office and PDR (113/114); PDR (115/116); 'New American Workplace' light-industrial definition with ancillary office, showroom and retail
Uber Advanced Technologies Group (113 West, 114, 115, 116) and Gusto (113 East) per the Port's January 2019 sublease list; STRUCTURE later describes 'two technology tenants'
Building 113-114 atrium (the 1914 connector) and the ~45,000 sq ft plaza framed with Building 14 are publicly accessible under Master Lease Exhibit K
Later additions Buildings 23 and 24 on the east end (1941 shed and washroom, ~1,500 gsf) removed to facilitate rehabilitation

Built as the Union Iron Works' machine, blacksmith and boiler shops; the Building 115 foundry produced over a million pounds of castings a month by 1919; 'Pacific Coast Steel Corporation' lettering survives on 115/116
